issues.failure_explanation: In Case 2 the proof drops the second Poisson-summation term as if it were dominated by e^{-T}. Its exponent is 4π²α/h (T+α log(δ/C)) = 4π²/σ √N₁, which for large σ is much smaller than T=σ α√N₁, so the term is not O(e^{-T}). The final quadrature bound still follows by comparing this term with the claimed σ>σ_opt rate, but the displayed equality to O(T^l e^{-T}) is false.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the false equality O(T^l e^{-T}) in Case 2 by the correct bound O(T^l e^{-T} + e^{-4π²α/h (T+α log(δ/C))}) and then compare this with the claimed σ≤σ_opt and σ>σ_opt rates.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem eq:quaderrthm contains an invalid intermediate bound. Since main convergence theorems rely on this quadrature-error estimate, their proofs are not complete as written, although the stated final rates can be recovered by retaining the second term.
issues.title: Incorrect asymptotic comparison in Case 2 of quadrature error proof
issues.why_classification: The repair is a local asymptotic comparison in the proof; it preserves all stated convergence rates and requires no new global argument.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem statement and the preceding bound use the fractional part (α) in the denominator 1−(α). In the proof of Theorem mainthm the denominator is replaced by 1−α. For non-integer α>1 this gives a different, generally invalid bound; for integer α=1 it divides by zero. The correct expression is already available in the preceding estimate.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace every occurrence of (1−α) in the proof of Theorem mainthm by (1−(α)), using the already established bound in \eqref{boundforEbar}.
issues.overall_effect: The written proof of Theorem mainthm fails for non-integer α>1 and for integer α. The theorem statement itself uses the correct fractional-part expression, and the repair does not change the claimed rates.
issues.title: Use of (1−α) instead of fractional part in proof of main theorem
issues.why_classification: The correction is local and forced by the preceding equation; it preserves the theorem's statement and convergence rates.
